claims.text: The initial Ti-6Al-4V surface has a native oxide layer.
Untreated Ti-6Al-4V has a baseline hardness of approximately 350 HV.
A DLC coating can be deposited on Ti-6Al-4V by PVD at substrate temperatures below 200 °C.
The proposed PVD process will produce a DLC film 2–5 µm thick.
The intervention will form a uniform, amorphous DLC film on the alloy surface.
The resulting DLC film will have a high sp³ carbon content.
The DLC film is hard and has low friction.
The DLC film increases the effective surface hardness of Ti-6Al-4V.
The DLC film reduces friction relative to untreated Ti-6Al-4V.
The coating minimizes penetration by abrasives.
Reduced abrasive penetration and friction inhibit wear during sliding or cyclic loading.
DLC-coated Ti-6Al-4V will exhibit an effective surface hardness exceeding 2000 HV.
DLC-coated specimens will have a statistically significant reduction in wear volume relative to untreated specimens under the specified tests.
The hardness and wear improvements will persist under moderate temperatures and cyclic loading.
Elevated temperatures or environments that rapidly oxidize DLC may diminish the improvements.
Existing literature supports high hardness and wear resistance for DLC coatings.
Coating adhesion problems may reduce the expected improvement.
Thermal mismatch at the coating–substrate interface may reduce the expected improvement.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires hardness exceeding 2000 HV, whereas the falsification rule only requires a twofold increase over the stated 350 HV baseline (about 700 HV). A result between about 700 and 2000 HV could fail the stated prediction without satisfying the hardness-failure criterion.

The hypothesis makes both a hardness claim and a wear-resistance claim, but the falsification rule uses an 'and' condition requiring both claims to fail. Failure of either central claim alone would therefore not formally falsify the combined hypothesis.
